description: We’re a team building a software-only entry for Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. Our tool uses NASA POWER climate data to help farmers compare crop rotations based on their soil, water and priorities. We’re looking for [roles, e.g. a front-end developer, someone with agriculture or earth-science knowledge, a designer for the pitch video]. We have [your skills]. Message us with your skills and availability for the 14–15 November event.
summary:
TerraAdapt is an installable web app that turns NASA weather, satellite, and soil data into field-specific guidance for farmers. A farmer can set a field’s location and choose a crop and sowing month, then explore how that crop might fare using past weather from that area. The app shows a plain-language season result, suggests better sowing months or alternative crops, and lets users compare plans in the Rotation Lab. Home and My Season put crop advice and risk information up front, while Ask Terra supports voice and text questions.

The project addresses Field Shift by making complex Earth data easier to use in local planting decisions. It shows evidence, uncertainty, and data gaps so users can judge how much to rely on its guidance. TerraAdapt is designed for fields around the world and includes built-in language options. Its scores are a teaching and decision-support index, not a forecast of actual yield.
details:
1. What does it do?

The farmer picks a language, then the app finds their location.

It reads 20 years of NASA weather and satellite greenness for that spot.

It simulates heat, cold-night and water stress for each crop.

The Rotation Lab ranks crop sequences, with the best months to sow.

A game replays a real season, including the worst year.

Terra answers questions by voice in the farmer’s language.

2. Benefits

Advice uses the farmer’s own spot, not a district average.

Risk is shown as colours and a growing crop, not as charts.

Every result names its data source and an evidence grade.

No sign-up and no cost.

3. Intended impact

Farmers see climate risk before spending on seed or water.

Better crop and timing choices lead to less loss in difficult years.

It reaches farmers who don’t read English.

4. Tools

Data: NASA POWER, NASA MODIS NDVI, Open-Meteo, SoilGrids, USDA SSURGO, OpenStreetMap.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-learn, SQLite.

Front end: JavaScript, three.js, Leaflet.

AI: local Ollama models, with Gemini as an optional fallback.

Built and tested on a laptop with Claude, Playwright and ffmpeg. Packaged with Docker.

5. Creativity

The farmer watches a real season grow or fail in their own weather.

The first screen is language, in each language’s own letters.

A “worst year in 20” replay at the farmer’s own field.

A small machine-learning model learns one place’s greenness and flags months worse than the weather explains.

6. Factors considered

Honesty: nothing is made up, and backup data is labelled.

Uncertainty: results carry an evidence grade, and they compare options without promising yield.

Access: language and voice first, no account needed; data stays on the device.

Cost: free local AI, with labelled backup weather if NASA is slow.

Safety: the AI key is never stored on the server, and it tells farmers to confirm with a local adviser.
